till-geochemistry-data.d: Till geochemistry surveys are targeted at regions of high mineral potential where glacial sediments cover and obscure the underlying bedrock. These surveys are conducted in conjunction with surficial geology mapping. British Columbia Geological Survey GeoFile 2017-09 provides the complete data set of publically available, regional-scale, till geochemical surveys. The surveys, carried out by the British Columbia Geological Survey, the Geological Survey of Canada, and Geoscience BC, compiles 39 reports released between 1992 and 2017, and includes geochemical data for 10,454 samples. Five Microsoft Excel tables generated from this database provide analytical determinations for the clay (<2 μm) and silt plus clay (<63 μm) size fractions of tills by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry after an aqua regia or modified aqua regia digestion, after a lithium metaborate fusion, and by instrumental neutron activation. These data tables can be brought into GIS software and integrated with other geoscience data to generate new exploration targets and design follow-up exploration programs. BCGS Open File 2019-04 is an index of geographically referenced, regional- and property-scale till geochemical surveys.
till-geochemistry-data.m: The Till Geochemistry 2017 compilation is an update to the Till Geochemistry 2007 compilation.

till-geochemistry-surveys.d: Till geochemistry surveys are targeted at regions of high mineral potential where glacial sediments cover and obscure the underlying bedrock. These surveys are conducted in conjunction with surficial geology mapping. British Columbia Geological Survey Open File 2019-04 indexes geographically referenced, regional- and property-scale subglacial till geochemical and mineralogical surveys targeting base and precious metals in British Columbia. It also lists topical studies relevant to drift prospecting in the province and elsewhere. Original source reports can be downloaded using the URLs provided, as can publications that use the data, such as compilations. The digital versions of the index enable advanced searches using fields such as author, source type (digital or PDF), or source. The survey index is released in PDF, ESRI Map Package, Shapefile, File Geodatabase, and KMZ formats. The Shapefile and KMZ formats are available with this catalogue entry. BCGS GeoFile 2017-09 provides the complete data set of available regional-scale, till geochemical surveys.

timing-windows-for-work-in-and-about-wat.d: Timing windows are the period(s) during the year when work may be carried out in and about water bodies with the lowest risk to fish and wildlife species and habitat. Timing windows and terms and conditions vary based on regional differences in fish and wildlife species and habitat, and geography. The timing window of least risk to fish and fish habitat must be applied to all activities in water bodies, as well as tributaries that have a risk of depositing sediment into water bodies. Windows of least risk are designed to protect all fish species known to occur in a water body.

timing-windows-for-work-in-and-about-wat.d:
This dataset is a generalized view of "Timing Windows for Work in and About Waterbodies in the Cariboo Natural Resource Region" used for viewing the data at the Regional level.

Timing windows are the period(s) during the year when work may be carried out in and about water bodies with the lowest risk to fish and wildlife species and habitat. Timing windows and terms and conditions vary based on regional differences in fish and wildlife species and habitat, and geography. The timing window of least risk to fish and fish habitat must be applied to all activities in water bodies, as well as tributaries that have a risk of depositing sediment into water bodies. Windows of least risk are designed to protect all fish species known to occur in a water body.

together-for-wildlife-strategy-project-i.d:
Together for Wildlife is the new provincial strategy to improve wildlife and habitat stewardship across British Columbia. It was built collaboratively through engagement with Indigenous peoples, rural communities, academic institutions, a wide range of stakeholder organizations, and the public. The strategy includes additional funding, proactive objectives, and improved data and knowledge – all supported by new policies, strong partnerships, and dedicated resources. This new approach commits to advancing reconciliation with Indigenous peoples through shared governance and mutual respect. The Together for Wildlife strategy includes 5 goals and 24 actions to achieve the vision that wildlife and their habitats thrive, are resilient, and support and enrich the lives of all British Columbians.

The dashboard displays information about provincial and regional projects that were funded by Together for Wildlife. Projects are associated with a particular goal and action under the strategy, and focus on the stewardship of wildlife species and their habitats, as well as related communications and engagement. Currently, the dashboard includes projects funded during 2020-2021, and additional years of data will be added annually.

The spreadsheet includes project information that forms the basis for the dashboard, such as the location, dollar amounts of funding, and achievements.

trade-in-services.d:
This data uses Statistics Canada estimates of international trade in services as a foundation. It estimates B.C.’s portion using a custom BC Stats methodology and presents the results in the same classification used by Statistics Canada’s annual international trade in services data release. Data is provided annually for different service categories and partner countries.

Services cover a wide variety of transactions on products that are generally intangible in nature. Unlike physical goods, services aren’t reported by customs officials when they cross political borders. Nevertheless, Statistics Canada produces estimates based on information from many sources. Statistics Canada’s groups services into four broad categories (commercial services, government services, travel services and transportation services) and numerous sub-categories.

translink-major-road-network.d:
The Major Road Network (MRN) supports the safe and efficient movement of people and goods across the Metro Vancouver region. It includes more than 600 kilometres of major arterial roads that carry commuter, transit, and truck traffic. The MRN connects the provincial highway system with the local road network, and some corridors also serve cyclists and pedestrians.

TransLink, in partnership with municipalities, plans the region's MRN. TransLink contributes funding for the on-going operation, maintenance and rehabilitation of the MRN, but ownership and operational responsibility for the MRN remains with the respective municipalities. TransLink also shares the cost of road, cycling, and pedestrian improvement projects with municipal partners and other stakeholders, in order to expand options for driving, cycling, and walking across the region.

translink-metro-vancouver-boundary.d: This data set shows the boundary of TransLink's service area, which aligns with the boundary of the Metro Vancouver region. It is a subset of the Municipal Boundaries data set downloaded from Metro Vancouver's Open Data Catalogue (http://www.metrovancouver.org/data).

translink-port-of-vancouver-facilities-t.d: This data set shows the location of Port of Vancouver facilities and marine terminals in Metro Vancouver. These include facilities operated by a number of different companies and in a variety of different sectors including: auto, bulk, break bulk, container, coal, grain, oil/chemical and passenger. The source of this data is the Port of Vancouver "Interactive Map", which can be accessed here: https://www.portvancouver.com/interactive-map

translink-temporary-road-closures.d: This data set shows longer-term, temporary road closures that impact goods movement in the Metro Vancouver region. In general, the closures are construction-related, have a duration of at least 3 months, and the location is on a designated municipal truck route or a road that is part of the Major Road Network (MRN) in Metro Vancouver.

translink-truck-parking.d: This dataset shows the locations of officially recognized truck parking facilities in Metro Vancouver. Data sources include the Province of BC and the City of Surrey (https://www.surrey.ca/city-services/791.aspx).

An Ungulate Winter Range (UWR) is defined as an area that contains habitat that is necessary to meet the winter habitat requirements of an ungulate species. UWRs are based on current understanding of ungulate habitat requirements in winter, as interpreted by FLNR regional staff from current scientific and management literature, local knowledge, and other expertise from the region. UWRs within this set of data are currently in the review and consultation stage of the area designation process.

As UWRs are designated they will be moved into the Approved Ungulate Winter Range (http://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/ungulate-winter-range) dataset.

urgent-and-primary-care-centres.d:
Urgent and Primary Care Centres provide a flexible resource to meet the urgent and primary health care need, primarily in large urban centres where a higher percentage of the population is unable to find or access a regular family doctor or nurse practitioner. As a resource to support communities, Urgent and Primary Care Centres are one of the mechanisms to immediately address the urgent and ongoing care needs of all patients within a community.

Urgent and Primary Care Centres are open to all patients in select communities. For example, they may become the regular clinic for patients without a family doctor or nurse practitioner until another practice or provider within the community can be identified. Urgent and Primary Care Centres also provide alternative care options for patients with a regular family doctor or nurse practitioner often unable to make same-day or next day appointments, and are designed to ensure continuity of care by communicating the relevant information back to a patient’s regular primary care provider.

Urgent and Primary Care Centres provide better access to same-day, urgent, non-emergency health care, including in the evening and on weekends. They provide an alternative to visiting emergency departments for issues that do not need to be seen in a hospital. For example, patients who require medical attention within 12 to 24 hours for something like a sprain, minor cut or burn can visit an Urgent and Primary Care Centre.

visitor-centre-network-statistics-progra.d: There are over 100 Community Visitor Centres and six provincial British Columbia Visitor Centres (BCVCs) located throughout the province. The Network of Visitor Centres provides visitor servicing to more than 3,000,000 visitors annually and is a valued partner in the distribution of tourism information and the promotion of industry products and services. Visitor Centres provide a full range of services that increase resident and visitor awareness of local, regional and provincial tourism products. These services also enhance the quality of the visitor's experience by promoting longer stays and/or return visits, thus maximizing the economic benefits to the community. Services provided by Visitor Centres typically include travel information and route planning, reservations, ticket sales and merchandise sales. The Visitor Centre Network Statistics Program Year Over Year Report 2012 contains aggregated data collected for all Visitor Centres (VC) over a two year period (2010 and 2011) and comparison percentages between the two years. The data indicates for each Visitor Centre the average number of parties per hour, total hours of operation, total tourism-related phone calls, total tourism-related written enquiries (by mail/fax/email), total number of parties who visited in person, total number of people in the visitor party (visitors), and total number of tour buses that stop at the a Visitors Centre.

walk-in-clinics-in-bc.d: Programs in BC that provide walk-in treatment services for people who have minor illnesses or injuries that do not require a visit to a hospital emergency department or an urgent care facility. These programs are generally specialized practices set up by groups of physicians operating within the provincial-territorial heath system who are available for patients that do not have family physicians or who need medical treatment and-or diagnosis at times when their family physician is not available. In some areas, a walk-in clinic may rotate between the clinics of different physicians. Some programs, mainly in major metropolitan areas, may operate on a 24-hour basis but all tend to be open for some or all evenings and weekends. water-approval-points.d:
The location (point) where an approval has been requested to conduct works in the vicinity of a water source.

Water Approvals are issued under the Water Sustainability Act (https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/14015) and are issued as either a Section 10 for Short Term Use of Water or a Section 11 for Changes in and about a Stream, depending on the type of proposed works. The Act and the Water Sustainability Regulation describe the type of works that are covered under each type of approval.

c: WATER APPROVAL ID is a system generated unique identifier number.
WSD REGION represents the water management region, e.g., West Coast.

APPROVAL TYPE is the type of approval as regulated under the Water Sustainability Act, i.e., STU (Section 10 Use Approval - Short term use of water), A-CIAS (Section 11 Change Approval - Changes In and About a Stream), N-CIAS (Section 11 Notification - Changes in and About a Stream).
APPROVAL FILE NUMBER is the file number assigned upon acceptance, e.g., 2004267.
FCBC TRACKING NUMBER is a system number generated by the FCBC tracking software, e.g., 100157672.
SOURCE is the stream name in which work will be occurring, e.g., Meadowbank Creek.
WORKS DESCRIPTION is a general description of the type of work to occur, e.g., Works within riparian zone.

QUANTITY is the quantity of water to be withdrawn from the source for a given purpose of use, e.g., 45.46. The majority of units are in cubic meters per day (CMD) but some may be cubic meters per second (CMS) or cubic meters per year (CMY).

PRECINCT is a jurisdictional area within a Water District. It is a combination of District and Precinct codes and names, e.g., 20E - New Westminster / Coquitlam. Not all Water Districts contain Precincts.
LATITUDE is the geographic coordinate, in decimal degrees (dd.dddddd), of the location of the feature as measured from the equator, e.g., 55.323653.
LONGITUDE is the geographic coordinate, in decimal degrees (dd.dddddd), of the location of the feature as measured from the prime meridian, e.g., -123.093544.

UTM ZONE is a segment of the Earth's surface 6 degrees of longitude in width. The zones are numbered eastward starting at the meridian 180 degrees from the prime meridian at Greenwich. There are five zones numbered 7 through 11 that cover British Columbia, e.g., 10.
UTM EASTING is the distance in meters eastward to or from the central meridian of a UTM zone with a false easting of 500000 meters.
UTM NORTHING is the distance in meters northward from the equator.

water-sustainability-temporary-protectio.d: Temporary Protection Orders (TPOs) are ministerial orders that can be implemented to curtail water users during times of water scarcity to protect streamflow availability for fish populations and the aquatic ecosystem. TPOs were implemented under Section 9 of the Fish Protection Act prior to 2016, but are now implemented under Section 86, 87 and 88 of the Water Sustainability Act. This dataset is a compilation of data hosted on TPOs to date across British Columbia and is maintained by the Watershed Stewardship and Security Branch within the Ministry of Water, Lands and Resource Stewardship. The purpose of the dataset is to communicate to water users when and where TPOs are/were in effect at the watershed scale. For specific details on which water users are affected by a TPO, please refer to the official Ministerial Order document referenced in the dataset.

watershed-condition-cariboo-thompson-oka.po: Land Use Planning and Cumulative Effects - Cariboo
watershed-condition-cariboo-thompson-oka.d:
The Cumulative Effects Framework (CEF) Watershed Condition Assessment provides a coarse-level, GIS-based approach for evaluating watershed condition. Assessment results represent the modelled condition of watersheds derived from spatial analysis, rather than field-based measurements. The results are intended to support strategic and tactical decision-making within the Cariboo and Thompson-Okanagan Natural Resource Regions and may also provide contextual information to inform operational decision-making.

The assessment is organized around four thematic areas that guide the evaluation process:
1. Streamflow Hazard - the likelihood of the occurrence of peak flow events
2. Sediment Hazard - the likelihood that fine sediments will be generated and delivered to streams
3. Riparian Function Hazard - the likelihood that there has been loss of or alteration to riparian vegetation causing reduced function of the riparian area
4. Ecological Importance (available for Cariboo Region only) - the importance of an assessment unit for fish and fish habitat.

Spatial data for current assessments can be downloaded via the links on the right-hand side of this BC Data Catalogue record. *Please note that spatial data for the Cariboo and Thompson-Okanagan Regions is provided as separate downloads. Some watersheds span both Regions, so there is some overlap between the datasets.*

wetland-and-riparian-potential-lower-fra.d:
The Wetland and Riparian Potential – Lower Fraser Valley dataset is a region wide assessment of wetland and riparian potential across British Columbia’s Lower Mainland summarized within a multi-scale H3 hexagonal grid framework (https://h3geo.org). The mapping can be used to reveal areas most conducive to wetland formation and is classified into four simplified categories: *Water*, *Wetland*, *Upland/Anthropogenic*, and *Potential Wetland*.

The dataset area encompasses the Lower Mainland region of British Columbia, specifically focusing on the area extending from the City of Vancouver eastward to the District of Hope. The dataset was generated using a comprehensive suite of high resolution terrain, hydrological, remote sensing, and land cover datasets (many derived from LiDAR and Sentinel 1/2 imagery) to characterize environmental conditions associated with wetland formation. Key input layers include topographic indices (Multi-scale Topographic Position Index - mTPI, Topographic Wetness Index – TWI, Normalized Digital Surface Model – nDSM), hydrologically enforced terrain models, depression and distance to water analyses, canopy height models, long term change detection, surface water dynamics, soil drainage classes, and 2021 flood extents. Modelling challenges included hydrologic enforcement in managed landscapes and modelling flow in low relief terrain.

white-sturgeon-fraser-river-drainage-mar.d:
This dataset includes White Sturgeon (Acipenser transmontanus) mark-recapture data collected in the Fraser River drainage. Users can use a Passive Integrated Responder (PIT) tag serial number to look up if the fish has been recaptured before and any associated data at last capture (e.g. fish length, girth, location, etc.).

This dataset is maintained by the Reconciliation, Lands, Policy and Data Division within the Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship (WLRS). Data and information housed within the database is collected by both government biologists and partners such as First Nations, scientific fish collection permit holders, and participating fishery organizations.

The [Fraser River drainage White Sturgeon PIT tag lookup app] (https://bcgov-env.shinyapps.io/sturgeon-pit-tag-lookup/) is also available as a tool to access this dataset.

wildlife-species-inventory-incidental-ob.d:
An incidental observation is a recorded detection of a species or its sign that was not a part of a formalized survey. This can occur when a non-focal species is observed during a survey for another species, outside of the study area, or as a chance observation made at random. Observations may include information on species, sex, age class, activity, and location.

The validity of these sightings is widely variable depending on the level of expertise of the observer and how visible the animal(s) was. This is the publicly available version of the incidental observation dataset. For the secured version of this dataset, 'Wildlife Species Inventory Incidental Observations - All' please see the BC Data Catalogue entry here .

Observations may result from various survey methodologies, such as stratified random block, distance sampling, reconnaissance, mark re-sight, wildlife camera traps, pellet group counts, and snow tracking.

This dataset contains the Province of British Columbia’s wildlife survey observation data for secured species occurrences that have been obfuscated (masked) to allow for public distribution in accordance with the Species and Ecosystems Data and Information Security Policy. It consists of polygons (grid cells) outlining the geographic areas where a secured survey observation has occurred. Each polygon in this dataset contains relevant information about the observation such as species and observation date, as well as instructions on how to request the source point location information for the observation.

wildlife-species-inventory-survey-observ.d:
This dataset contains the Province of British Columbia’s ungulate survey observations originating from the Species Inventory (SPI) database, including both secured and publicly available point locations. An observation is made when a surveyor makes a visit to a Design Component (block, transect, sample station) on a specific date at a specific time and enumerates the target species or its sign. Observations may include information on count, species, sex, age class, activity, and survey conditions. Observations may result from various survey methodologies, such as stratified random block, distance sampling, reconnaissance, mark-resight, wildlife camera traps, pellet group counts, and snow tracking. Each observation may be geo-referenced individually or by association with a specific Design Component.

The majority of ungulate survey observations are publicly available in the 'Wildlife Species Inventory – Survey Observation Points – Ungulates – Publicly Available' dataset. However, some observations are secured in accordance with the Species and Ecosystems Data and Information Security Policy (SEDIS).

'Wildlife Species Inventory - Masked Survey Observations - Publicly Available' contains wildlife survey observation data for secured species occurrences that have been obfuscated (masked) to allow for public distribution in accordance with the Species and Ecosystems Data and Information Security Policy. The masked layer may be used to approximate where secured point data for …

wildlife-species-inventory-survey-summar.d:
This spatial view contains the Province of British Columbia’s publicly available summary data from wildlife surveys stored in the Species Inventory (SPI) database. Survey Summary data are summaries of observation data in specific geographic areas. This dataset consists of polygons outlining the geographic areas that have been surveyed. Each polygon may have summarized information for wildlife populations such as a population counts or estimates, age-class ratios, sex ratios, correction factors, and confidence limits. Summary data may result from various wildlife survey methodologies, such as stratified random block, distance sampling, reconnaissance, mark-recapture, wildlife camera traps, pellet group counts, and snow tracking, among others.

Some summary data are not presented in this layer because they are secured in accordance with the [Species and Ecosystems Data and Information Security Policy.]

[Species and Ecosystems Data and Information Security Policy.]: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/natural-resource-stewardship/laws-policies-standards-guidance/data-information-security
To request access to secure data available in Wildlife Species Inventory - Survey Summary - Secured please submit a request to the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy using the contact information provided below.

wildlife-species-inventory-telemetry-poi.d:
Radio-telemetry of wildlife may be defined as the transmission of information from a transmitter on a free-ranging wild animal to a receiver. Wildlife-related telemetry is also known as radio tagging, radio-tracking. Advances in the field of wildlife telemetry have made it possible to acquire detailed data on many aspects of wildlife biology, including habitat use, home range size, mortality and survivorship, and migration timing and routes. Since many wildlife species are secretive and difficult to observe, radio-telemetry has provided a valuable tool to learn more about their respective life histories.

Most species and ecosystems data and information in B.C. data systems are available online to the public, consistent with B.C.'s Open Information and Open Data Policy. Data and information which are routinely secured are noted in the ‘List of Species and Ecosystems Susceptible to Persecution or Harm’. Secured data is managed and distributed in accordance with the Species & Ecosystems Data & Information Security (SEDIS) policy. For the current list of species and ecosystems that are considered susceptible to persecution or harm and for more information on SEDIS see here .

For information on the secured dataset see Wildlife Species Inventory - Telemetry Points - All .

williamson-s-sapsucker-wisa-.d:
Williamson’s Sapsucker (WISA) data; includes the three distinct Areas of Occupancy (AOs), WISA Habitat Model, WISA Observations and Nest Trees. These data support the implementation of the Williamson's Sapsucker Best Management Practices (BMPs).

1. Area of Occupancy: 95% of the WISA population is estimated to occur in this area and is where the WISA Best Management Practices (BMPs) apply.

2. BMP Habitat Classes: Polygons delineating class 1 habitat (highest quality), class 2 habitat, and areas where no habitat has been found. The BMPs have specific harvest practices outlined for class 1 and 2 habitat.
1. Class 1 and Class 2 habitat in the West and Okanagan-Boundary AOs is based on the habitat model for WISA. To facilitate spatial analysis, all subtypes of Class 1 habitat areas were subsumed to a single data class titled Class 1 within column BMP in the attribute table of the habitat model. More details on the BMP Habitat Classes can be found in the BMP document and the guiding principles document that accompanies the BMPs.
2. Class 1 and Class 2 habitat in the East Kootenay AO is based on a combination of the habitat model for WISA and buffers around existing and probably nest sites and more details on the BMP Habitat Classes can be found in the BMPs and the guiding principles document that accompanies the BMPs.
